rationale:
M14 ONTOLOGY (2026-10-04), the `implements` type, and the replacement for a RULING THAT WAS PROSE. The doc said: 'C++ has no separate interface construct: interface satisfaction IS inheritance, and inheritance is emitted as extends. There is no `implements` keyword, no `implements` clause, and no distinct base-class list to read.' Two of those three sentences are true and the conclusion is wrong. There is indeed ONE base-class list — but a base with at least one PURE VIRTUAL member (`virtual int read(char*, int) = 0;`) IS C++'s interface (Core Guidelines C.120, 'prefer using abstract interfaces as NVI'), and `implements` names WHICH base is a contract and which carries state, which `extends` does not. Corpus measurement, from `script/cpp-review/ontology-census.ts`: 127 pure-virtual members across 26 files, 28 classes declaring at least one, 171 (derived -> contract) pairs, 12 of them in this lane's own cpp-example corpus. So the ruling is FALSIFIED by the corpus, which is precisely the failure mode `ontology-coverage-gate.ts` was written for — `overrides` was ruled on prose for a whole wave and the differential stayed green because the oracle was written after the ruling.

Four negative arms, each a shape that a looser rule would swallow, and each measured on the pinned grammar rather than guessed:
  - a virtual WITH A BODY (`virtual int read(...) { return 0; }`) is not pure: `Derived2 : ReaderLike` gets `extends` and NO `implements`.
  - a DEFAULTED ARGUMENT (`virtual int width(int n = 0)`) puts its `=` inside the `parameter_list`, not on the declaration, so `UsesDefaulted : Defaulted` is not a contract. The same argument on a method DECLARATION (`virtual int width(int n = 0);`, a `field_declaration`) is a second, separate arm: `UsesDeclaredDefaulted : DeclaredDefaulted`. It is here because the mutation run needed it — the first version of `cpp/ontology-pure-virtual-subtree-scan` SURVIVED against the definition form alone, because `isPureVirtualDeclaration` refuses a `function_definition` before it looks at any children. A negative arm that cannot fail is documentation, and the run said so.
  - a MEMBER INITIALIZER (`int counter = 0;`) is a `field_declaration` with an `init_declarator` and no function declarator at all, so `Derived3 : WithInit` is not a contract.
  - `Plain` has no base, so there is nothing to implement.

And the ordering arm, which is the whole of the rule's correctness rather than a detail: `ForwardDerived` is written BEFORE the `LaterInterface` it implements. A rule that emitted at the base-clause node would resolve nothing yet, so the candidate is RECORDED there and ADJUDICATED after the walk from the whole-file pure-virtual registry. `cpp/ontology-implements-order-dependent` is the mutant that moves the emission back to the base-clause node, and it must die on THIS row alone: the other three positive pairs have their bases declared ABOVE them and stay green under the mutation.

ONE ARM OF THE PURE-SPECIFIER READ IS REDUNDANT, and the mutation run said so rather than leaving it as an apparent gate. `isPureVirtualDeclaration` requires a `function_declarator` child, but it is reached only from the class-scope METHOD branch, so a member initializer (`int counter = 0;`, which on the pinned grammar IS a `field_declaration` carrying an unnamed `=` and a `number_literal 0` — the same two nodes a pure specifier has) never arrives at it. A mutant removing that requirement therefore SURVIVED. It is kept as defence in depth and its rationale says what would be required to break it; the mutant that does bite is `cpp/ontology-pure-virtual-subtree-scan`, which attacks the load-bearing half (the `=` must be a DIRECT child, so a defaulted argument inside a `parameter_list` cannot qualify).

WHY `extends` AND `implements` BOTH fire for `Concrete -> Reader`: the family rule that forbids a duplicate row is about one FACT stated twice (containment, an include dependency). These are two facts about the same base clause — 'inherits from' and 'implements this contract' — and only the second tells a consumer that `Reader` carries no state it could inherit. Emitting one and calling it coverage would be the prose ruling again.

expectRelationships.note: the contract base: `read` is pure, `seek` is virtual-with-a-body, and `fd` is state — only the pure member makes it an interface, and the edge records WHICH one so a consumer can re-derive the verdict.
one edge per (derived, base) PAIR: `Both` implements two contracts and that is two facts, not one edge with two targets.

THE ORDERING ARM. The base is declared 24 lines BELOW the derived class, so at the moment the base clause is read the registry does not yet know `LaterInterface` is a contract. Recorded-then-adjudicated, not emitted-there. This row is the ONLY one that dies under `cpp/ontology-implements-order-dependent`, which is why it is here and not implied by the other three.
`extends` is NOT withdrawn for a contract base. Both labels describe one base clause and answer different questions; see the rationale.

expectRelationshipCount.note: one edge per pair, as an EXACT count — `expectRelationships` means '>= 1 match', so only `equals` can fail on a duplicate.

forbidRelationships.note: NEGATIVE ARM: `ReaderLike::read` is virtual WITH a body, so the base is a base class and not a contract. Emitting here is the over-firing direction, and it is the direction that makes `implements` mean nothing.

NEGATIVE ARM: a DEFAULTED ARGUMENT is not a pure specifier. `virtual int width(int n = 0)` has no `= 0` on the declaration, and reading it as one would make every defaulted-int function a contract member.
NEGATIVE ARM: a MEMBER INITIALIZER is not a pure specifier. `int counter = 0;` has no function declarator.
NEGATIVE ARM: `Plain` declares NO base, so there is nothing to implement and no such edge may exist.
a class cannot implement itself — the D2 self-base refusal carries to the new label, and a self-edge here would be the same fabrication D2 measured at 49 rows.

NEGATIVE ARM, the one the mutation run needed: a DEFAULTED ARGUMENT on a class-scope method DECLARATION. `virtual int width(int n = 0);` is a `field_declaration` whose `function_declarator` holds an `optional_parameter_declaration`, and the `=` + `0` sit INSIDE that parameter_list — a `= 0` two levels down, which is what a subtree scan finds. The definition form above cannot catch this, because that node is a `function_definition` and the predicate refuses it first; that is why BOTH arms exist and why the subtree-scan mutant dies on this row and not the other.
